items.title: Learning Cannot Be Delegated: Why the Division of Cognitive Work Between Learners and Generative AI Should Shift Over Time

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.

items.title: The Invisible Harm Doctrine: Structural AI Harm And Neurodivergent Cognitive Liberty

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive liberty as a complementary normative formulation, not an existing legal right and not a replacement for present neurorights frameworks. It states the principal objections to the doctrine and responds to them, and it concludes by identifying research, design, and governance questions necessary to evaluate whether and how these harms can be detected, challenged, and mitigated. The article does not report new primary data, establish clinical efficacy, or propose a ready-to-adopt legal standard.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: In April 2026, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Clinicians (CfC) alongside HealthBench Professional (HBP), an open benchmark evaluating large language models (LLMs) on real clinician chat tasks across 3 domains: care consult, writing and documentation, and medical research. These releases could represent a significant step toward incorporating AI into clinical settings and warrant evaluation by radiologists. We critically analyzed HBP’s methodology, results, and implicit claims, with particular attention to what the benchmark reveals about AI performance in radiology workflows. Also, we examined the benchmark design, performance data across models, the physician baseline, and key limitations relevant to imaging informatics and academic radiology practice. HBP offers a rigorous, openly reported benchmark of AI performance in the clinical setting. However, radiology is underrepresented in the data set; its sampling strategy, which favors difficult and adversarial cases, means its absolute scores cannot be interpreted as real-world performance rates. Because HBP uses difficult and adversarial red-teaming cases, and the benchmark authors state its score is “not percent accuracy,” the finding that the CfC system outscores the physician baseline (59.0 vs. 43.7) should be read as a benchmark-conditional result under intentionally hard sampling, not as evidence that the system is superior to physicians in routine care. For radiologists and radiology AI researchers, this benchmark is a useful yet incomplete evaluation of LLMs’ capabilities in imaging informatics. In addition, HBP is a text-based benchmark of clinician chat tasks that does not assess image interpretation; therefore, its relevance to radiology is mostly confined to documentation, communication, and evidence-retrieval workflows.

items.title: Negotiating AI at work: motivational tensions and the redefinition of marketing expertise

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial Intelligence Marketing (AIM) tools are increasingly transforming how marketing work is performed. However, its impact on individual practitioners remains underexplored. This study aims to examine how marketing professionals experience and negotiate the contradictory motivational consequences of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled work. Rather than treating AI as either empowering or threatening, the study explores how these effects coexist and how practitioners respond to them. Design/methodology/approach Twenty in-depth interviews were conducted with marketing practitioners using an exploratory, theory-informed qualitative design. Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs, Self-Determination Theory and the Job Characteristics Model were used as complementary sensitising lenses to orient interpretation, while coding procedures informed by grounded theory techniques were used to develop themes inductively from the data. Findings The findings reveal that AIM simultaneously empowers and destabilises practitioners. AI enhances efficiency, capability, strategic focus, confidence and creative possibilities, while also generating uncertainty regarding task ownership, professional identity, technological dependence and future relevance. These effects are not experienced as separate outcomes. Instead, practitioners continually negotiate competing tensions by reframing expertise, selectively integrating AI, preserving human control over consequential tasks and reaffirming distinctively human sources of professional value. Motivation therefore emerges as dynamic and continually reconstructed rather than as a stable outcome of AI adoption. Research limitations/implications The design prioritises interpretive depth rather than statistical generalisability. Future research could develop measures of AI-enabled empowerment, destabilisation and negotiation using larger and more diverse samples. The research sample did not analyse differences across career stages, and warrants future investigation. This paper examines broad AIM tools rather than isolated technologies. Future studies should explore how particular AI capabilities change dimensions of professional value and motivation. The findings highlight negotiation as a continuing process, but the cross-sectional design provides only a snapshot of the process. Longitudinal research could establish whether empowerment-destabilisation tensions persist, intensify, diminish or change form over time. The findings suggest potentially important roles for trust, employee participation, work design, organisational support and AI governance. Future research could investigate the organisational conditions that facilitate productive negotiation of AI-related tensions for marketing practitioners. Practical implications Organisations should consider: Evaluating AI in terms of how it changes employees’ experiences of expertise, ownership, autonomy and professional value; Approaching AI capability development as workforce transformation, rather than technical training alone; Preserving meaningful human ownership of work; Addressing the efficiency-intensification paradox. Providing employees with meaningful agency over AI adoption; Treating AI governance as a crucial part of the employee experience. Social implications AI simultaneously empowers and destabilises marketing practitioners, generating tensions around expertise, autonomy, identity and employability. Rather than passively accepting change, individuals actively negotiate these tensions through adaptation, reframing and human–AI collaboration. AI’s long-term impact will depend not only on technological capabilities, but also on how organisations sustain meaningful work, professional development and human agency. Originality/value This study contributes a new tension-based framework that explains how motivation is continuously constructed under AI-driven work environments. In addition, it advances the understanding of AI-enabled work in three ways. Firstly, it conceptualises employee motivation as shaped by simultaneous empowerment and destabilisation rather than by uniformly positive or negative effects. Secondly, it shows how AI redefines marketing expertise from task execution towards judgment, interpretation, contextual understanding and human–AI orchestration. Thirdly, it identifies ongoing negotiation as a central process through which practitioners sustain professional value and motivation under technological change.

items.venue: Higher Education, Skills and Work-Based Learning
items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper argues that the institutional response to employer concerns about graduate unreadiness constitutes a misdiagnosis. Current employability frameworks are dismantling the critical thinking and cross-cultural competencies that graduates, and the labour markets they enter, most need. The paper repositions universities as irreplaceable sites for developing cognitive and intercultural capacities that neither employers nor artificial intelligence can generate independently. Design/methodology/approach The paper analyses Australian higher education policy, accreditation frameworks, ranking systems and national data documenting the decline of Asian Studies. Drawing on scholarship on employability, critical thinking and intercultural competence, and on the implications of artificial intelligence (AI), it uses the Australian case to show how structural incentives drive curricular drift away from foundational intellectual development. Findings Accreditation and accountability frameworks have produced cumulative drift toward narrow vocational competencies at the expense of critical thinking and cross-cultural competence. The collapse of Asian Studies in Australia shows how employability metrics undervalue preparation whose benefits are long term. Post-pandemic graduates are entering AI-shaped labour markets that most demand the capacities universities have spent decades quietly removing. Originality/value The paper frames the employability paradox, showing that the institutional cure is worsening the condition it claims to treat. Its original contribution is to connect the decline of Asian Studies, the logic of accreditation and the demands of AI-enabled workplaces in a single policy argument with direct implications for universities, accreditors, policymakers and teachers.

items.venue: International Journal of Law and Management
items.abstract_text: Purpose Reasoning-capable language models and retrieval-augmented generation are already changing how legal work gets done, yet Indonesia’s judicial and advocacy institutions have barely begun to reckon with what that change means. This study aims to ask two things. First, what these two technologies actually add to legal research, drafting and adjudication support, once the marketing claims are set aside. Second, what governance Indonesia needs so the tools strengthen rather than erode due process, confidentiality and access to justice. Design/methodology/approach The method is normative-juridical, drawing on statutory, conceptual and comparative analysis of primary legal materials from Indonesia, the European Union, the USA, the UK, Singapore and China, read alongside recent empirical studies of legal-AI hallucination. Findings Retrieval grounding measurably reduces hallucination in legal output, but it does not eliminate it and the error rate that remains is still higher than any court would tolerate in a human-drafted filing. Three existing provisions of Indonesian civil and electronic-systems law already offer partial traction on that risk, but Indonesia’s dedicated governance for AI in legal practice sits scattered across a nonbinding 2023 ethics circular, a Presidential Regulation still waiting for a signature, an Advocate Law under constitutional-court-ordered revision and a judicial ethics code that has never once mentioned algorithms. Originality/value This article proposes a four-layer framework built on statutory duties, executive regulation, professional self-regulation and practice-level safeguards, names the institutional obstacles each layer will face and argues that without deliberate attention to cost and access, the same framework could hold the country’s legal-aid clients to a lower standard of reliability than its paying ones.

items.title: Before and after ChatGPT: longitudinal evidence on academic writing transformation in higher education research

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Applied Research in Higher Education
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines whether the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly following the public release of ChatGPT, is associated with measurable changes in academic writing within higher education research. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal corpus of 461 higher education journal articles published between 2018 and 2025 was constructed using openly accessible PubMed data. Computational text mining and natural language processing techniques were employed to extract linguistic features, including word count, sentence length, lexical diversity, AI-related terminology, hedging expressions, certainty expressions, and a composite Academic Writing Transformation Index (AWTI). Descriptive statistics, independent-sample t-tests, interrupted time series regression, hierarchical regression, robustness checks, and effect size analyses were conducted using R. Findings The findings reveal a gradual yet measurable transformation in academic writing following the emergence of ChatGPT. Post-ChatGPT articles contain significantly more AI-related terminology, longer texts, and higher AWTI scores, while lexical diversity decreases, suggesting greater linguistic standardization. Interrupted time series analysis indicates that these changes reflect progressive adaptation rather than an immediate structural shift. Originality/value This study moves beyond perception-based accounts by providing longitudinal evidence of changes and continuities in the linguistic characteristics of published higher education articles following the public release of ChatGPT. Its originality lies in distinguishing the diffusion of AI-related terminology from broader linguistic change through an integrated framework combining computational linguistic indicators, interrupted time-series analysis and the AWTI.

items.title: Managing uncertainty in generative AI interactions: a resource depletion perspective

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Despite significant investments from organizations, generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) is still not widely used for deeper knowledge production and transformation. Existing research has focused on external constraints (infrastructure, skills and governance) to explain Gen AI withdrawal behaviors, while paying little attention to the internal psychological states that users go through when interacting with Gen AI. Design/methodology/approach This study investigates how users’ cognitive and emotional resources are depleted by the interactional uncertainty present in Gen AI and how this depletion influences withdrawal behaviors associated with Gen AI by utilizing conservation of resources theory (COR). Data are analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling from a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of 317 users. Findings The findings show that interactional uncertainty is positively associated with both cognitive and emotional resource depletion. Cognitive resource depletion has a positive association with knowledge feedback withdrawal but does not influence non-transformational use, whereas emotional resource depletion increases non-transformational Gen AI use but does not affect feedback withdrawal. Furthermore, the effect of cognitive – but not emotional – resource depletion is moderated, and non-transformational usage is directly decreased by perceived value. Originality/value The study contributes theoretically by extending COR to the Gen AI context and practically by offering guidance on designing Gen AI systems that support sustained and transformative knowledge use.

items.venue: Journal of Information, Communication and Ethics in Society
items.abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine associations between perceived academic integrity climate and students’ anticipated ethical dissent intention in a simulated competitive artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled workplace context. The model evaluates direct associations and indirect associations through perceived AI literacy, digital moral disengagement and moral awareness. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 489 Indonesian university students was analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Perceived AI Literacy was assessed through self-report items concerning understanding of AI limitations, risks, ethical appropriateness and appropriate use. Anticipated Ethical Dissent Intention was assessed through a standardized workplace vignette designed to present ethically salient workplace pressures consistently across respondents. The construct therefore represents stated intention under simulated conditions rather than observed workplace conduct and is interpreted as anticipated rather than enacted ethical dissent. Findings Perceived academic integrity climate was positively associated with anticipated ethical dissent intention and perceived AI literacy and negatively associated with digital moral disengagement. Perceived AI literacy showed the largest direct association with anticipated ethical dissent intention. The indirect association through perceived AI literacy was substantially larger than the serial indirect association through digital moral disengagement and moral awareness. The serial indirect coefficient was statistically different from zero but substantively negligible. Practical implications The findings support greater institutional attention to clear integrity expectations, responsible AI guidance and evaluative AI capability in higher education. These implications identify educational priorities rather than demonstrated effects on subsequent workplace conduct. Originality/value The study integrates perceived academic integrity climate, perceived AI literacy, digital moral disengagement and moral awareness within a model of anticipated ethical dissent intention under a simulated AI-enabled workplace scenario. The contribution lies in identifying a theoretically coherent pattern of associations within Indonesian higher education rather than demonstrating causal preparation for subsequent workplace conduct.

items.title: When executable AI advice backfires: feasibility, managerial reliance, and strategic performance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This paper examines how the feasibility of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated advice shapes managerial reliance, firm performance, and trust in strategic decision making. It distinguishes advice quality from execution reliability, defined as the probability that an attempted AI-backed action avoids an implementation-failure loss. Design/methodology/approach The study develops a parsimonious expected utility model with stochastic source choice in which managers choose between human judgment and AI advice under demand uncertainty and competitive interaction. The model separates expected operating value, implementation feasibility, and accountability cost. A repeated duopoly simulation is then used to examine how changes in AI feasibility affect reliance, performance, and trust. Findings Higher AI feasibility increases managerial reliance, but its effects on performance and trust are conditional. Under the baseline state-based recommendation and payoff-space source-choice rules, high feasibility increases reliance by 20.08 percentage points and reduces average payoff by 0.242 relative to low feasibility. AI-only trust updating produces rising trust paths in every regime, but average trust is 0.064 lower under high feasibility. Performance turns positive when AI execution reliability is very strong relative to a weak human routine. Raising the state threshold substantially attenuates the effects. Originality/value The study positions feasibility as a first-order governance variable. Source substitution when human and AI recommendations agree accounts for most of the baseline performance loss.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose This study examines how academic librarians in Nigeria experience and manage emotional labor when they integrate generative artificial intelligence (AI) into reference services, and how that labor is carried out through epistemic work. Design/methodology/approach A constructivist grounded theory study was conducted in three academic libraries (federal, state and private) in Kwara State, Nigeria. Twenty-one reference, liaison and systems librarians took part through semi-structured interviews, non-participant observation of AI-mediated reference consultations and artifact analysis. Data were analyzed through initial and focused coding, constant comparison and memo writing. Findings Reference librarians' anxiety centered on professional credibility, liaison librarians' on bias in AI outputs and systems librarians' on technical instability. Librarians managed these feelings through two forms of epistemic work: epistemic vigilance, the alertness that sets how closely an output is checked, and epistemic stewardship, the verification and correction done to protect patrons. Trust calibration linked this work to the confidence librarians could honestly show patrons. Critical incidents restarted the cycle, and its burden was heavier where policy, training and technical support were thin. Originality/value The study proposes epistemic emotional labor as a construct for knowledge work mediated by AI. It extends Hochschild's account of emotional labor to algorithmic mediation, shows how infrastructural inequality shapes that labor in a Global South setting and identifies an affective and epistemic omission in current AI literacy guidance for library workers.

items.abstract_text: Purpose As a contribution to The Practice of Making Decisions, this paper presents an AI-assisted strategic posture instrument that helps equity analysts and portfolio managers examine the strategic assumptions underlying an investment thesis by assessing alignment among environmental demands, strategic ambition and execution capability. items.abstract_text: Purpose This article aims to provide a scoping literature review about qualitative empirical studies on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare, with a specific focus on chronic condition management. Given the growth of chronic diseases, the proliferation of AI-based systems and the lack of in-depth empirical research, the review critically examines the contributions, assumptions and weaknesses of major research perspectives in this domain. Design/methodology/approach A scoping literature review was conducted, focusing on 24 qualitative studies addressing the implementation and use of AI in chronic disease management. The analysis was structured using interpretive metaphors as a heuristic lens to categorize how AI is framed across different studies. Findings Three key metaphorical themes were identified: (1) AI as artificial guardian; (2) AI as oracle; and (3) AI as replicant. Drawing on these results, we argue that a distinction emerges between contributions that consider “AI in healthcare practice” – emphasizing AI as an entity that intervenes providing solutions – and “AI as healthcare practice” – highlighting the role of these systems as dynamic, contextual and socially constructed and embedded elements. Originality/value This review offers a novel contribution by applying interpretive metaphors to critically synthesize qualitative studies on AI in chronic disease management. The employed metaphors can provide insight into how AI is framed by researchers, and the roles and implications scholars envision for these systems within healthcare contexts. The findings also outline future research directions, highlighting the need for a more nuanced and interdisciplinary understanding of the complexities and socio-technical aspects of AI in healthcare. items.title: From compliance to resilience: a functional framework for AI-enabled environmental governance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in corporate environmental governance, yet much of what is labelled AI in this context is difficult to distinguish from conventional rule-based digital automation. Its contribution so far has concentrated on automating compliance reporting rather than building the adaptive capacity that resilience thinking requires. The paper defines what qualifies as AI-enabled environmental governance and develops a framework for distinguishing AI-enabled compliance from AI-enabled resilience, with particular attention to enterprises in middle-income, small and medium enterprise (SME)-dominated economies undergoing simultaneous digital and green transformation. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual paper takes a theory-synthesis approach, combining a technical definition of AI systems with resilience theory, the technology-organization-environment framework and research on greenwashing and AI-washing to propose a four-layer framework: sensing, decision, institutional and equity. Each layer's level of analysis and candidate operational indicators are specified, its relationship to existing digital-maturity models is clarified and its boundary conditions are set out. The central sensing-to-decision mechanism is illustrated with secondary case evidence and examined alongside independent survey-based studies from South and Southeast Asia, whose findings are consistent with, though not a direct test of, the proposed mechanism. Findings The paper argues that AI investment concentrated in the sensing layer, without corresponding investment in the decision and institutional layers, produces compliance-grade rather than resilience-grade outcomes. This pattern is expected to be most pronounced in resource-constrained, SME-dominated settings, where sensing tools can be purchased as point solutions while decision-layer integration requires internal capability that is harder to build. Independent survey evidence from medium enterprises in Indonesia and from the banking sector in India is consistent with this asymmetry, although neither study was designed to test the framework directly. Practical implications The framework offers regulators, firms, financial institutions and educators a vocabulary and a set of candidate indicators for distinguishing genuine resilience investment from compliance automation, useful for designing tiered, capability-aware policy instruments during the current transition towards harmonized international sustainability disclosure standards. Social implications Because environmental shocks fall hardest on those least able to absorb them, the distribution of AI-enabled resilience capability across firms of different sizes is a question of social equity and not only of technical efficiency. The framework's equity layer treats this distribution as a design variable that regulators, financiers and educators can act on, rather than as an unintended side effect of technology diffusion. Originality/value The paper supplies a technical definition of AI-enabled environmental governance and identifies a specific governance failure mode: a layer-specific asymmetry in the cost and purchasability of AI capability that predicts where disclosed adoption and substantive practice are likely to decouple. items.abstract_text: Abstract Governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in courts has largely focused on the conditions of responsible use, including accuracy, transparency, contestability, confidentiality, and human oversight. This article addresses a different question: When should judges refuse, postpone, or sharply limit AI assistance even when a system is sufficiently reliable and subject to ordinary safeguards? It argues that algorithmic restraint is a distinct, role-specific judicial virtue: the stable disposition to preserve the non-delegable conditions of judgment by bearing the professional and institutional costs of non-use when regulated use cannot do so. The article develops a three-stage framework that examines the system and mode of reliance, the adequacy of safeguards, and whether AI use would substitute for an act constitutive of adjudicative responsibility. This framework yields a restraint ladder ranging from verified informational use to categorical abstention. Applications to credibility assessment, predictive tools, legal research, summarization, and AI-assisted drafting show that the argument does not depend on general human superiority. Rather, it asks whether AI can improve judicial decision-making without displacing the judge’s responsibility to hear, evaluate, reason, and remain answerable for the exercise of public authority.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Cloud computing security is a major concern of organizations as their sensitive data is being managed on an off-premises platform. Several factors, such as the cloud’s layered architecture, its dynamic environment, and dealing with unseen or zero-day attacks, lead to a complex and challenging security environment. Existing Intrusion detection system (IDS) solutions often focus on a single cloud layer and rely solely on machine learning models, which may perform well on benchmark datasets but remain limited when evaluated across heterogeneous cloud monitoring layers. This study proposes an adaptive confidence-aware multi-layer intrusion detection framework using reinforcement learning for network, host, and hypervisor environments. An XGBoost model is employed at each layer to detect known attacks, while prediction confidence thresholds calibrated via the Q-learning algorithm (layer-wise) are employed to separate reliable decisions from uncertain low-confidence events. Low-confidence cases are then passed to the Chroma memory-matching gate. The unresolved events are further escalated to Large language model (LLM) for semantic analysis and explanation. Final attack promotion is performed using calibrated LLM confidence thresholds, while a weighted-fusion fallback mechanism is available for low-confidence ATTACK predictions. Events that remain unresolved after this process are retained in a review bucket to avoid forced classifications. Confirmed attack knowledge and generated explanations are stored in ChromaDB to support future analysis and incremental retraining. Experimental results show that the proposed framework autonomously learns layer-specific confidence thresholds of 0.79, 0.78, and 0.73 for the Network intrusion detection system (NIDS), Host intrusion detection system (HIDS), and Hypervisor layers, respectively. Across the complete 15,000-event evaluation set, the fixed 0.85 static baseline produces 3,111 would be LLM escalations. In the adaptive cold run, this workload is reduced to 2,714 actual LLM calls. After confirmed attack knowledge is stored in ChromaDB, the warm run resolves 2,068 uncertain events through memory matching and reduces actual LLM calls to 646. This corresponds to a 76.20% cold-to-warm LLM-call reduction and a 79.24% reduction compared with the static baseline workload. Under the complete 15,000-event warm-run evaluation, the framework achieves 94.63% accuracy, 94.10% precision, 93.79% recall, and 93.95% F1-score.

items.title: Do AI Systems Zone Out? Functional Homeostasis and Graceful Degradation in LLM Agents under Cognitive Load

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract A tired person staring out of a window is not processing the scene; the eyes are open, but the input is not being handled. The behavior is protective: the system sheds load before it fails. This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) agents have a functional analogue. We introduce the concept of functional homeostasis : observable self-monitoring, load regulation, protective disengagement, and recovery under stress, with no claim of consciousness. We build COGLOAD, a benchmark of multi-thread operations tasks with hidden critical invariants and controlled context, latency, and token-budget stress, and evaluate three production models across four conditions: baseline, overload, overload with a homeostatic protocol (HAP), and overload with an engineering governor. In the main experiment, baseline success is 97%. The collapse is model-specific: two of three models truncate under overload, while one answers all batches at the smaller budget. Under output-budget pressure, 63% of runs hit the output cap and returned truncated, unusable output; only 37% were valid, critical recall fell to 37%, and no overloaded run declared that it had omitted work. A homeostatic protocol restored validity to 87% and made omission explicit in 87% of runs, but preserved only 41% of the original batches; a content-blind governor preserved 35%. The positional analysis shows the "zoning out" pattern directly: the models answered only the first few batches (mean index 2.4-3.0 of 20), and no answered batch came from the second half. We then specify HAP and derive design rules for agent runtimes: load telemetry, explicit degradation actions, invariant preservation, checkpointing, and recovery. The results suggest that the right question is not whether AI systems "feel" tired, but whether they can be designed to fail softly, report honestly, and recover quickly.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasks faster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledge they would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences of LLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studies remained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work. Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experienced workers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than ten studies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work, impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lowerself-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track performance. Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiency gain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose a framework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

items.abstract_text: Background The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has raised concerns about its relationship with students’ critical thinking, yet empirical findings remain inconsistent. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and Cognitive Offloading Theory, this study examined the competing indirect associations between GenAI tool use and self-reported critical thinking through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading. It also investigated the sequential indirect association involving both mediators to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cognitive-regulatory processes associated with GenAI-supported learning. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 378 undergraduate students from 10 universities in Jiangsu Province of China. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling (CB-SEM). Bias-corrected bootstrap analysis with 5,000 resamples was performed to examine direct, indirect, and total associations, as well as to compare the magnitudes of the competing indirect pathways. Results GenAI tool use was positively associated with self-regulated learning ( β = 0.431, p &lt; 0.001) and cognitive offloading ( β = 0.390, p &lt; 0.001). Self-regulated learning was positively associated with critical thinking ( β = 0.368, p &lt; 0.001), whereas cognitive offloading was negatively associated with critical thinking ( β = −0.409, p &lt; 0.001). Self-regulated learning was also negatively associated with cognitive offloading ( β = −0.318, p &lt; 0.001). The direct association between GenAI tool use and critical thinking was not statistically significant ( β = −0.059, p = 0.316). Bootstrap analysis identified a positive indirect association through self-regulated learning ( B = 0.147, 95% CI [0.096, 0.212]), a negative indirect association through cognitive offloading ( B = −0.148, 95% CI [−0.219, −0.092]), and a positive sequential indirect association through self-regulated learning and cognitive offloading ( B = 0.052, 95% CI [0.030, 0.088]). The total association was not statistically significant, and the two single-mediator indirect associations did not differ significantly in magnitude. Conclusion The relationship between GenAI tool use and critical thinking may be more complex than a uniformly beneficial or detrimental association. The findings reveal the coexistence of positive and negative indirect associations involving self-regulatory processes and cognitive offloading, highlighting the relevance of self-regulated learning in understanding how students engage with GenAI-supported learning. These results underscore the importance of supporting students’ self-regulatory capacities while encouraging thoughtful engagement with AI-generated information. Given the cross-sectional design and self-reported measures, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to clarify the temporal relationships among these constructs and their implications for critical thinking development.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) produced explanations, diagrams and worked solutions in seconds, which raised a pedagogical dilemma: better task completion did not show that learners had practised the reasoning needed for independent performance. This conceptual paper examined the intersection of spatial reasoning, scientific reasoning and critical thinking in AI-supported higher education. A focused, illustrative synthesis of research on spatial cognition, cognitive offloading, human-AI interaction and educational scaffolding identified a plausible mechanism of concern: when AI supplied both a representation and its interpretation, students could bypass the construction, transformation and checking of mental models. The paper distinguished supportive from substitutive offloading and proposed SPARC (Sketch, Predict, Audit, Reconstruct, Calibrate), a five-stage instructional sequence that preserved learner-generated spatial and causal reasoning while using AI as a fallible comparison partner. Two teaching vignettes from introductory physics, the vertical motion of a tossed ball and work and power in stair climbing, showed how the sequence could be implemented with brief written or visual artefacts and assessed with an illustrative rubric. Four falsifiable propositions and a feasible pilot design were formulated for classroom evaluation. SPARC was not presented as an empirically validated intervention, and the available studies did not establish that GenAI necessarily caused durable declines in critical thinking. The paper concluded that educational evaluation should examine unaided transfer, reasoning quality and confidence calibration, rather than the quality of AI-assisted products alone.

quarantine.title: “AI Knows English Better Than Me”: Multilingual EFL Learners’ Identity Negotiation and Emotional Well-being in the GenAI Era
quarantine.abstract_text: This inquiry examined how multilingual EFL learners in Tanzanian education negotiate language learner identities and emotional experiences when using GenAI tools for English learning. Data were gathered through focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews with 24 students from two public universities in Tanzania. Thematic analysis revealed three patterns of use. First, participants experienced heightened identity dissonance when comparing their English to GenAI-generated output, feeling inadequate due to postcolonial language hierarchies. Second, students practiced strategic identity protection by limiting GenAI use to low-stakes tasks and avoiding identity-significant writing. Third, emotional well-being was ambivalent: while GenAI reduced anxiety about grammar and vocabulary, it increased imposter feelings and shame, especially among students who saw GenAI reliance as betraying family sacrifices and personal effort. The findings challenge technosolutionist narratives portraying GenAI as neutral where English signifies colonial prestige and mobility, and Gen AI risks reinforcing linguistic hierarchies.

quarantine.abstract_text: The growing use of intelligent Internet of Things (IoT) systems requires embedded chip frameworks that can execute real-time learning, analytics, and secure inference under stringent energy, latency, memory, and reliability requirements. Nevertheless, current Edge AI offerings focus primarily on model compression or accelerator-level optimization, with limited attention to unified hardware-aware inference selection, energy-saving execution, and secure execution monitoring. This study presents HARE-EdgeChip, a hardware-aware, reconfigurable Edge AI chip framework for intelligent IoT systems. The proposed architecture includes sensor-level feature encoding, multi-path adaptive inference, neural execution based on INT8 quantization, lightweight on-chip learning, energy-aware scheduling, and secure trust monitoring. The framework dynamically selects lightweight ML, quantized neural, or compact temporal deep-learning inference paths based on workload complexity, energy availability, memory usage, latency deadline, and the security deviation score. Real-time IoT sensor workload experimental validation indicates that the proposed framework achieves 96.8% accuracy, 96.4% F1-score, and 97.1% secure-anomaly detection rate, while reducing inference latency from 13.8 to 7.9 ms, energy consumption from 5.9 to 2.6 mJ per inference, and memory usage by 48.6% compared to traditional embedded deep-learning baselines. These findings prove that HARE-EdgeChip is a reconfigurable, energy-efficient, secure, and scalable solution to next-generation intelligent IoT analytics.
